reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a persistent sensation of rocking, swaying, or bobbing that continues after returning to stable ground following passive motion, most often a sea voyage or long flight
The perceived self-motion is typically relieved, at least temporarily, by re-exposure to passive motion such as driving a car
Unlike motion sickness, there is usually no nausea or vertigo, and the dominant complaint is the internal sense of movement
Diagnosis is clinical and requires exclusion of vestibular, neurological, and other causes of imbalance
Symptoms lasting only days after travel are common and self-limiting; the syndrome proper is diagnosed when the rocking persists for weeks or longer
Vestibular rehabilitation and habituation strategies are central to management, and stress or fatigue tends to aggravate symptoms
It is thought to reflect a failure of the brain to readapt from the motion-adapted state back to a stable environment
reference.pathophysiology: Mal de debarquement syndrome is understood as a disorder of central vestibular adaptation. During sustained passive motion the brain adapts its internal model of self-motion and postural control; on return to a stable environment this adaptation normally reverses quickly, but in MdDS the maladaptive state persists, so the person continues to perceive rocking or swaying. Re-exposure to motion transiently restores the adapted state and eases symptoms, which supports a central sensory reweighting mechanism rather than peripheral vestibular dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral vestibular disorders (e.g. vestibular neuritis, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo)
Ordinary motion sickness or transient post-voyage unsteadiness
additionalInvestigations: Detailed clinical history linking onset to a period of passive motion
Neurological and vestibular examination to exclude central and peripheral disease
Audiometry and vestibular function testing where a peripheral cause is suspected
Brain imaging (MRI) if focal neurological features or atypical presentation
Assessment for migraine and psychological contributors
redFlags: Focal neurological signs suggesting a central lesion
True rotational vertigo, hearing loss, or tinnitus pointing to a vestibular disorder
Progressive or asymmetric symptoms atypical for MdDS
Severe functional impairment or associated mood disturbance
reference.prognosis: Many cases that follow travel resolve spontaneously within days to weeks, but a proportion become persistent and can wax and wane over months to years; vestibular rehabilitation and habituation help, though a subset have a chronic, relapsing course.
pitfalls: Confusing MdDS with ordinary motion sickness or peripheral vertigo
Failing to note the characteristic relief with re-exposure to motion
Missing vestibular migraine or persistent postural-perceptual dizziness as alternatives
Under-recognising the impact of stress, fatigue, and anxiety on symptoms
management: Vestibular rehabilitation and habituation exercises are the mainstay, retraining central vestibular adaptation
Reassurance and explanation, with early expectation that many travel-triggered cases resolve spontaneously
Avoid habitual re-exposure to passive motion as a coping strategy despite its transient relief, and manage stress and fatigue that aggravate symptoms
Optic-flow readaptation protocols, using full-field visual stimulation synchronised to head roll, in specialised centres for persistent cases
Pharmacological adjuncts targeting central mechanisms, such as a benzodiazepine (clonazepam) or an SSRI/SNRI, for symptom relief, with treatment of coexisting migraine
Address psychological comorbidity such as anxiety and depression with cognitive behavioural therapy and support
Neuro-otology referral with confirmation of the diagnosis by excluding vestibular and neurological causes

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of Mal de debarquement syndrome

nodes.text: Persistent rocking sensation after a period of passive motion such as sea or air travel
Red flag present (focal neurological signs or true vertigo with hearing loss)?
Escalate: neuro-otology review for central signs or atypical features
Clinical history, neurological and vestibular examination, audiometry if indicated
Does the rocking persist for weeks with vestibular and neurological causes excluded?
Consider vestibular migraine, postural-perceptual dizziness or peripheral vertigo
Reassure that travel-triggered cases often settle
Manage stress and fatigue that worsen symptoms
Clonazepam or an SSRI or SNRI for severe symptoms
Many resolve within days to weeks; some persist for months to years
